To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) high dietary lipid levels induced subcutaneous fat deposition, 2) lipid levels in muscle remained unaffected by dietary fat levels, 3) hepatic lipogenic enzymes were not affected by dietary lipid levels, 4) no protein sparing effect by dietary lipid level, 5) no effect on flesh quality.
high dietary fat levels did not affect flesh quality of turbot.
high dietary lipid levels affect growth and whole body chemical composition of turbot, but they induce very few alterations in muscle composition, and consequently in flesh quality.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of dietary lipid levels on growth performance, body composition, lipogenesis, and flesh quality of turbot.
the effects of dietary lipid level on the growth, body composition, hepatic lipogenic enzyme activities and flesh quality of turbot (Pestta maxima).
the effect of high dietary fat on growth, nutrient utilization, flesh quality and lipid deposition in turbot.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
turbot are not a fatty fish species.
the dietary fat level should be kept below 20% in turbot diets.
the dietary fat level should be kept at 15% for optimal growth of turbot.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
turbot can be fed diets containing 20% of fat without any detrimental effect on flesh quality.
dietary fat levels up to 20% can be used for turbot without affecting flesh quality.
dietary lipid level has little influence on flesh quality of turbot.
The main takeaway from our work is that
high dietary lipid levels did not compromise flesh quality and therefore, turbot can be considered as a species with low susceptibility to lipid oxidation.
high dietary lipid levels are not a concern for turbot flesh quality.
high fat levels are well tolerated by turbot and that the flesh quality of turbot is very robust.
